extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and policymakers interested in political philosophy and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying principles for when the state should or should not interfere with individual actions, private relations, and public functions, with attention to education, family power, bureaucracy, and central/local administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom cannot include the right to relinquish future freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of freedom cannot require that a person should be free not to be free; it is not freedom to be allowed to alienate one's freedom (e.g., by selling oneself into slavery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing absolute disposal of one's fundamental liberty defeats the justification for permitting individuals to pursue their own good; voluntary surrender of freedom that forecloses future freedom undermines the presumption in favour of liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on enforceability of contracts affecting personal relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Engagements which involve personal relations or services should never be legally binding beyond a limited duration of time; e.g., marriage has peculiarity that requires nothing more than the declared will of either party to dissolve it (per Humboldt's thesis as discussed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While legal enforceability may be limited, the full context—including moral obligations and consequences for third parties—must be weighed before deciding legal duration; the text notes this is complex and not decidable on very simple grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligations arising from inducing reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person, by promise or conduct, has encouraged another to rely on his continuing to act in a certain way (building expectations), new moral obligations arise which cannot be ignored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such induced-reliance obligations may justify limiting freedom to retract a promise or relationship; courts and moral assessment should account for expectations and stakes placed on that reliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of third-party consequences in deciding enforceability
rubrics_metrics.description: If the relation between contracting parties has produced consequences for others (placed third parties in peculiar positions or created them), obligations arise toward those third persons that affect whether and how the original relation may be dissolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These third-party interests don't necessarily require forcing fulfilment of the contract at all costs, but they must be given proper weight and affect moral (and sometimes legal) freedom to retract.

rubrics_metrics.name: State must control exercise of private power over others (family example)
rubrics_metrics.description: The State, while respecting individual liberty in matters concerning the person, is bound to maintain vigilant control over any power an individual is allowed to exercise over others—this is especially neglected in family relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law should give wives the same rights and protection as other persons; the State should not accept the plea of 'liberty' to justify despotic private power within families.

rubrics_metrics.name: State responsibility to protect children's interests against parental power
rubrics_metrics.description: Misapplied notions of liberty are an obstacle to the State fulfilling its duties toward children; parental absolute control should not prevent the State from intervening in education and welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The State ought to recognise and, where necessary, legally enforce obligations of parents to provide for children's education and upbringing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory minimum education up to a standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The State should require and compel the education, up to a certain standard, of every citizen (children), including examinations to ascertain basic abilities (e.g., ability to read).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement mechanisms could include fixed-age examinations, fines on parents (worked out by labour if needed), and mandating school attendance at parental expense if no excuse is shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use public examinations to enforce minimum knowledge, limited to facts and positive science
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent state influence over opinion, knowledge required for passing examinations (beyond instrumental skills) should be confined to facts and positive science; examinations on religion/politics should test knowledge of opinions, not require professing belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher-branch examinations should be voluntary; examinations should certify knowledge without compelling doctrinal positions; the State should avoid using exams to bias citizens' conclusions on disputed subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificates/ degrees should indicate competence but not create exclusionary state gatekeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Degrees or public certificates should be given to all who present themselves for examination and pass, but such certificates should confer no advantage over competitors other than public opinion's regard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It would be dangerous for governments to exclude persons from professions (e.g., teaching) on alleged deficiency of qualifications enforced by the State; certification should not be used to bar entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: State may enforce or provide services when private enterprise cannot
rubrics_metrics.description: When society is backward or private enterprise cannot or will not provide necessary institutions (e.g., schools, joint-stock companies for great works), government may, as the less of two evils, undertake the task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State provision is justified when private alternatives are unavailable; but this does not justify state direction where capable private providers exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bringing children into existence without adequate prospects is morally culpable; state may regulate marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: To bring a child into existence without fair prospect of providing both material and intellectual prospects is a moral crime against the offspring and society; laws forbidding marriage unless parties can show means of support do not exceed legitimate powers of the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such regulations may be expedient depending on local circumstances; they are framed as prohibiting acts injurious to others and may be social offences even absent legal punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three objections to non-liberty government interference to weigh
rubrics_metrics.description: When government action does not involve infringement of liberty, objections may be: (1) individuals are better suited to do it; (2) doing it individually is desirable for citizens' education and development; (3) adding unnecessarily to government power is harmful (the most cogent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision whether government should act must balance these three considerations—efficiency, civic development, and dangers of increasing centralized power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concentration of talent and functions in the bureaucracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Absorbing principal ability of the country into the government is dangerous: it creates dependence on bureaucracy, crushes independent criticism, and makes reform difficult even for rulers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To maintain a skilful and innovative bureaucracy, the State must not monopolize occupations that form and cultivate the faculties required for government; there must be opportunities outside government for forming and testing talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: State should decentralize power but centralize information and its diffusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical principle: the greatest dissemination of power consistent with efficiency; but the greatest possible centralisation of information, and diffusion of it from the centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Municipal/local administration should have wide local discretion and elected officers; a central organ should collect, concentrate, and diffuse lessons and experience, have the right to know what is done, and limited power to compel local obedience to general rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central superintendence: information, advice, limited coercion, appeal routes
rubrics_metrics.description: A central administrative organ should focus on gathering and sharing information, advising localities, and compelling adherence to laws where necessary; where rules are violated it should appeal to tribunals or to constituencies to dismiss errant officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Its actual power should be limited to enforcing laws and supervising execution; in matters not covered by general rules, local officers should use their own judgment under responsibility to constituents.

rubrics_metrics.name: State should enable varied private experiments rather than impose uniform education/administration
rubrics_metrics.description: A general State education is a contrivance for moulding people alike; the State's proper role is to allow multiple competing experiments and keep others to a standard by example and stimulus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State-run education, if it exists, should be one among many competing systems; excessive state control leads to despotism of the mind and loss of individuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: State activity should aid and stimulate individual exertion, not substitute for it
rubrics_metrics.description: Government cannot have too much activity of the kind which aids, stimulates, informs, and enables individuals; the mischief begins when it substitutes its activity for that of individuals or bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer policies that inform, advise, and when necessary denounce, rather than taking over and doing the work themselves; preserve opportunities for individuals to form practical experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power expansion as a check on when to avoid government functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every function superadded to government increases its influence over hopes and fears, attracting ambition and creating hangers-on; this growth of power is itself a strong reason against unnecessary government interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the long-term political effects of enlarging government functions: concentration of roles may lead to a bureaucracy that resists change and dominates public life; avoid adding powers unless essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong central coercion may be justified in cases of first-rate national interest
rubrics_metrics.description: In matters of paramount national interest (e.g., curing rooted maladministration that creates pauperism), powers of administrative coercion and subordinate legislation may be right and necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such powers should be sparingly used and limited to cases where local mismanagement produces harms beyond the locality and affects the nation as a whole.
